candidates.title: Enhancing the Ability of Consumers To Control the Robocalls
candidates.raw_excerpt: In this document, the Federal Communications Commission (Commission) modifies rules to ensure that consumers can revoke consent for robocalls they no longer wish to receive while continuing to receive those they still want. candidates.title: Someone Ran a Chemical Analysis of Bodega Retatrutide and Dear Lord
candidates.raw_excerpt: Like gas station kratom, research-grade peptides have become widely available for consumers at convenience stores across the United States. Yet as one investigation into peptides sourced from a New York City bodega found, ease of access comes with a high price: your health. In new reporting on the peptide trade, CBS took a hard look at gray market peptide products available across the US, including a knockoff of Eli Lilly’s yet-to-be-released injectable weight loss drug retatrutide, bought from a corner store in Brooklyn. To test what’s actually in a bodega vial labeled “retatrutide,” the news outlet sent samples to Jason Galpin, a researcher of bioorganic chemistry at the University of Iowa. His analysis? “It does not look anything like a peptide,” he told CBS . In place of any sort of peptide-like-substance — which should be made up of short chains of amino acids — Galpin discovered the vial was chock full of phenylacetic acid, a filler-compound typically used in perfume and illicit amphetamine manufacturing . Worse yet, the vial also contained at least 13 various bacterial colonies, which director of development at the University of Iowa’s Center for Biocatalysis and Bioprocessing Carl Ross told CBS could easily cause a dangerous infection. “As kids, we’re all taught to wash out cuts if we get cut,” Ross explained. With gray market peptides, however, users are “injecting bacteria under the skin where it could multiply. It’s pretty terrifying.” Last month, Wired conducted a similar analysis, buying “peptides” from a bodega in Brooklyn and sending them to a lab for analysis. As with CBS, it turned out that they weren’t peptides at all; instead, they found chemical slurry that technicians couldn’t even identify. So there you have it: if your guy at the corner deli tries to slip you some peptides to go with your chopped cheese, just say no. Your body will thank you — in more ways than one . candidates.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
candidates.raw_excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film. When they saw the images for the first time, the scientists were literally jumping up and down with joy. This photo is the first view of Earth from space taken by a camera on a U.S. Army V-2 rocket launched from White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico on Oct. 24, 1946. The magnitude-7.0 earthquake that struck Baqen County in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region late on Thursday was an extensional rupture inside the Qiangtang block, about 2 kilometers from the Baqen-Leiwuqi fault, the China Earthquake Networks Center (CENC) said.

The finding, released on Friday as rescuers worked across the high-altitude epicentral area, explains a counterintuitive feature of the event: the plateau is being squeezed, yet this fault was pulled apart.

"Simply put, an extensional rupture means the crust is stretched along a horizontal direction," said Han Yanyan, a senior engineer at the center's earthquake forecasting department. "Under tension and gravity, the upper block slides down along an existing fault, forming fractures."

The India-Eurasia collision lifted the plateau and thickened its crust, and the interior is subject to both north-south compression and east-west extension, producing two sets of faults that run roughly north-south and east-west.

candidates.raw_excerpt: Black holes more massive than entire galaxies are not a major component of the mysterious dark matter that's thought to make up most of the matter in the cosmos, a new study finds. For decades, to explain why galaxies do not spin apart at the speeds at which they whirl, scientists have suggested the existence of an unseen substance known as dark matter , whose gravitational pull helps keep galaxies together. Dark matter is thought to make up about five-sixths of all matter in the universe . Much remains unknown about dark matter, however — including whether or not it actually exists. Black holes make good potential contenders for dark matter, since they are extremely massive and are difficult to spot in the dark depths of space. candidates.raw_excerpt:
Buildings have digital twins in the cloud-based platform, underground utility tunnels are monitored in real time, and traffic lights adjust to changing road conditions. In the Xiongan New Area in north China's Hebei Province, these futuristic scenarios have been part of everyday life.

A digital foundation for an intelligent city

Often referred to as a "city of the future," Xiongan is China's first city to develop its digital and physical infrastructure simultaneously across the entire area. Early in the planning phase, the city embraced a concept of building "three cities" together – a city underground, a city above ground and a city in the cloud.

The Xiongan Urban Computing Center serves as the "brain" of the digital city, providing essential support for the development of a digital urban environment. It supplies computing, storage and network services for the entire digital twin city, enabling integrated urban planning, unified construction supervision and coordinated city governance through a shared digital platform.

"If the digital twin city is a tree, the computing center is its roots and soil," said Liu Yao, manager of the information system department at the Xiongan Cloud Network Technology Co., Ltd.

The center currently supports more than 100 categories of urban operational data from over 20 government departments in Xiongan, covering six major dimensions, including geospatial information, Internet of Things (IoT) sensing and government services.

candidates.title: Europe's Space Rider vehicle comes crashing down during drop test
candidates.raw_excerpt: Europe has dropped the ball on the prototype for its first reusable spacecraft. Or, rather, the prototype itself was dropped — on purpose — but the outcome of its fall was not what engineers had hoped for. The incident occurred during an Oct. 6 drop test of the full-scale Space Rider model , from the European Space Agency (ESA). The robotic vehicle's initial drogue parachute deployed successfully, but its main parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow its descent before crashing into the ground, according to ESA officials. The cause of the failure remains under investigation. "Following several successful tests using representative vehicle masses, the latest system-level drop test in October was not completed as planned due to an anomaly during the parafoil deployment sequence," an ESA spokesperson confirmed in an email to Space.com. "An independent investigation is ongoing to determine its root cause and inform the next steps." Space Rider is being developed as Europe's first reusable orbital spacecraft — an uncrewed vehicle designed to carry scientific experiments to orbit for up to two months, then return them to Earth for analysis. Its method of return, though, differs from that of any other spacecraft in operation today. Space Rider''s wingless, lifting-body design relies on a steerable parachute, or parafoil, to maneuver toward its landing area. This allows it to perform runway-style touchdowns, as opposed to other, less accurate parachute-aided recoveries in current practice. This month's drop test was intended to demonstrate that ability, which is a critical requirement for Space Rider's planned reuse after missions in orbit, but the impact of its failure may not end up disrupting its ultimate development timeline.
